lessons.0.slides.1.title: The Scale and Global Landscape of the Auction Market
lessons.0.slides.1.content: **Market Scale** — The global wine auction market traded approximately $500–700 million in 2026, of which: Burgundy accounts for 30–40 % (roughly $200–250 million); Bordeaux accounts for 25–30 %; Burgundy investment-grade wines have grown at an annual compound rate of 8–12 %. **Market Function** — Auctions are the core of the secondary market, providing: price discovery (transparent bidding forms market consensus); a rapid liquidity channel for collectors selling rare old vintages; access to rare wines (90 %+ of old vintages are only available at auction); and a market benchmark influencing retail pricing and investment decisions. **Historic Milestone** — In October 2018, a bottle of 1945 DRC Romanée-Conti fetched **$558,000** at Sotheby's, setting the world record for a single bottle of wine and symbolising Burgundy's peak position in the investment market.

lessons.0.slides.7.title: The Role and Services of Auction Houses
lessons.0.slides.7.content: Auction houses are not merely trading platforms — they also provide: authenticity verification (by specialists); valuation services; storage and logistics; insurance arrangements; and market reports. Top auction houses such as Sotheby's have dedicated wine departments staffed by Masters of Wine. They reject lots with questionable provenance, protecting buyers and sellers alike. Commission is the principal source of revenue.

lessons.1.slides.1.title: Preparation Before the Auction
lessons.1.slides.1.content: **Six Essential Steps for First-Timers**: 1️⃣ **Registration**: provide identity proof (passport/ID) and financial proof (credit card statement or bank letter of recommendation); some high-value auctions require a deposit ($10K–50K). 2️⃣ **Obtain the Catalogue**: released 2–3 weeks ahead (printed or digital); study each lot description, estimate, and bottle condition carefully; mark lot numbers of interest. 3️⃣ **Preview Inspection**: open 3–7 days before the auction; personally inspect bottle condition, fill level, and labels; photograph and ask the auction house specialist. 4️⃣ **Set a Budget Ceiling**: calculate total cost including commission (+25 %); write down the maximum bid for each lot; enforce discipline — never exceed it. 5️⃣ **Research Historical Sale Prices**: use Wine-Searcher for past prices for the same vintage; reference the Liv-ex index; observe auction trends over the past 3 years. 6️⃣ **Choose a Bidding Method**: floor bidding, telephone commission, or online; experienced buyers may spend weeks preparing or even hire an adviser.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 📖 Case Study: First-Time Auction Participation
lessons.1.slides.2.content: **Case: Mr. Chang's First Acker Hong Kong Auction** — Background: Mr. Chang wanted to buy 2015 DRC La Tâche, budget NT$150,000. Preparation (3 weeks ahead): registered with Acker, provided credit card details; received the digital catalogue; found Lot 888: 2015 DRC La Tâche (1 bottle); estimate HK$32,000–38,000 (~NT$128K–152K); condition: IN fill level, perfect label, original wooden case. Research: Wine-Searcher showed retail ~NT$180K; past 3 auction results: HK$35K, HK$36K, HK$34K; decided ceiling: HK$38,000 (with commission ~NT$190K — over budget but acceptable). Preview day: inspected the lot in person; fill confirmed IN, label perfect, case original; specialist: 'This came from a prominent collector with perfect storage.' Auction day: chose online bidding (could not attend in person); started at HK$28,000, rose by HK$1,000 increments; fierce competition; placed a decisive bid at HK$37,000 — **won!** Settlement: hammer price HK$37,000; buyer's premium 22 %: HK$8,140; total: HK$45,140 (~NT$180K); wired payment within 24 hours; arranged professional transport to his cellar in Taiwan. Result: acquired the dream bottle below retail, perfect condition, clear provenance. Slightly over budget, but Mr. Chang felt it was worth it — and the experience built his confidence for future auctions.

lessons.1.slides.5.title: 📚 Complete Glossary of Auction Terms
lessons.1.slides.5.points.0: Lot: a single bidding unit; may be 1–12 bottles or a full case
lessons.1.slides.5.points.1: Hammer Price: the price at which the auctioneer's hammer falls; excludes commission
lessons.1.slides.5.points.2: Reserve Price: the seller's minimum price; lot is unsold if not reached
lessons.1.slides.5.points.3: Estimate: the auction house expert's assessed range; typically conservative
lessons.1.slides.5.points.4: As-Is: sold as is; no quality guarantee; no returns after the fact
lessons.1.slides.5.points.5: Buyer's Premium: additional 15–25 % paid by the winning bidder
lessons.1.slides.5.points.6: Seller's Commission: 10–15 % paid by the seller
lessons.1.slides.5.points.7: Provenance: the history of a wine's storage and ownership
lessons.1.slides.5.points.9: Inspection Recommended: suggests potential condition issues
lessons.1.slides.6.title: Auction Rules and Legal Obligations
lessons.1.slides.6.content: **Core Rules** — Bidding is binding: once you raise your paddle or click 'bid', it is a legal commitment that cannot be retracted. Winning bids cannot be cancelled: you must pay as promised — defaulting results in being blacklisted. Payment deadline: typically full payment within 24–72 hours (wire transfer or credit card). As-Is clause: buyer accepts condition risk. Authenticity guarantee: most auction houses offer a 5-year authenticity guarantee (keep all documentation). **Consequences of Default** — Permanently blacklisted by the auction house; house may pursue the price-difference loss; credit record damaged, other houses may refuse; severe cases may face legal action. **Dispute Resolution** — Condition disputes: must be raised within 7 days of receipt; authenticity disputes: can apply for a refund within 5 years; arbitration is preferred over litigation.

lessons.2.slides.0.description: Judging fair prices and investment value
lessons.2.slides.1.title: A Systematic Approach to Price Valuation
lessons.2.slides.1.content: **Three Key Valuation Dimensions**: 1️⃣ **Historical Sale Price Analysis** — Search auction records for the same vintage and producer over the past 3 years; calculate average and standard deviation; observe price trend (rising/falling/stable); tools: Wine-Searcher Pro, Liv-ex, auction house sale records. 2️⃣ **Retail Market Comparison** — Use Wine-Searcher to find global retail prices; compare 5–10 major merchant quotes; remember retail price usually includes service and guarantee; auction price + commission should be at or below retail to make sense. 3️⃣ **Bottle Condition and Provenance Assessment** — Perfect condition can command a 20–50 % premium; a famous-cellar provenance can add 30–100 %; OWC adds 10–20 %; large formats (Magnum) add 50–100 %. **Price Relationships** — Rare old wines: auction > retail (10–30 %); standard bottles: auction ≈ retail; bulk lots: auction < retail (wholesale discount).
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 📊 Case Study: 2015 DRC La Tâche Price Valuation
lessons.2.slides.2.content: **Valuation Target**: 2015 DRC La Tâche (1 bottle, 750 ml); auction: Acker Hong Kong, March 2026; estimate: HK$32,000–38,000. **Step 1 — Historical Sale Prices** — Past 3-year records: Dec 2025: HK$35,000 (Zachys); Sep 2025: HK$36,500 (Sotheby's); Jun 2025: HK$34,000 (Acker); 2024 range: HK$32K–38K → **Average: HK$35,000**. **Step 2 — Retail Market Price** — Wine-Searcher: HK$42,000–48,000 (Hong Kong merchants); US: $5,200–5,800 (~HK$40K–45K); Europe: €4,500–5,200 (~HK$38K–44K) → **Average retail: HK$43,000**. **Step 3 — Bottle Condition Assessment** — Catalogue: IN fill level (perfect), label intact and legible, OWC, provenance: prominent Hong Kong collector, professional cellar storage → **Perfect condition, premium warranted**. **Synthesis** — Estimate HK$32K–38K is fair (below retail); historical average ~HK$35K; add 22 % buyer's premium: HK$35K × 1.22 = HK$42,700 — close to the low end of retail, reasonable. **Bidding Strategy** — Target: HK$36,000 (with commission HK$43,920); hard ceiling: HK$38,000 (with commission HK$46,360); above HK$38K abandon (approaches retail high end; auction advantage lost). **Conclusion**: HK$32K–36K is a fair bidding range; above HK$38K is poor value.

lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🍾 Complete Fill-Level and Condition Guide
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: IN (Into Neck): fill level within the neck — perfect; no premium issues
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: BN (Base Neck): fill at the base of the neck — normal; acceptable
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: TS (Top Shoulder): fill at the top of the shoulder — acceptable for old wines; 0–10 % discount
lessons.2.slides.5.points.3: HS (High Shoulder): fill level low; rising risk; 20–30 % discount
lessons.2.slides.5.points.4: MS (Mid Shoulder): mid-shoulder fill; significant oxidation risk; 40–50 % discount
lessons.2.slides.5.points.5: LS (Low Shoulder): low fill; very high risk; 60 %+ discount or unsold
lessons.2.slides.5.points.6: Label: intact (no discount) → slight damage (–5–10 %) → severe damage (–20–30 %)
lessons.2.slides.5.points.7: Cork: dry or signs of seepage → significant deduction; may be refused
lessons.2.slides.5.points.8: OWC: 10–20 % premium; demonstrates provenance and storage

lessons.2.slides.7.points.6: Case verification: vintage and lot number match the bottles; original factory seal

lessons.3.slides.0.title: Bidding Strategy and Risk Management
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 17 min
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Systematically Formulating a Bidding Plan
lessons.3.slides.1.content: **Before the Auction — Your Operating System**: Step 1 — Build a target list: review the catalogue and identify 10–20 lots; categorise them as core targets (must-win), secondary targets (optional), and opportunistic lots (bargain hunting); note lot numbers, estimates, and condition. Step 2 — Set price ceilings: research historical sale prices for each lot; calculate true cost including commission (hammer price × 1.22–1.25); write down the absolute maximum for each lot — mark it in red and keep it in front of you during bidding. Step 3 — Budget allocation: example total budget NT$500,000; core targets: 60 % (NT$300K); secondary targets: 30 % (NT$150K); opportunistic lots: 10 % (NT$50K). Step 4 — Schedule: auctions typically run 4–6 hours with 400–600 lots; estimate when your target lots appear; schedule breaks to avoid fatigue-driven decisions. Step 5 — Prepare alternatives: if a primary target fails, pivot immediately to the alternative; don't chase losses emotionally; remember: another auction will come. **Golden Rule**: Better to go home empty-handed than to overpay for a single bottle.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 😱 Failure Lessons: Three Fatal Mistakes Beginners Make
lessons.3.slides.2.content: **Case 1 — Losing Rational Thinking When Competition Heats Up**: Mr. Lee, 35, tech industry. Target: 2005 DRC Romanée-Conti; budget: NT$800,000 (incl. commission); estimate: HK$160,000–180,000 (~NT$640K–720K). Auction day: the bidding started at HK$140K and rapidly climbed — HK$170K, HK$180K, HK$190K, HK$200K. His original ceiling was HK$165K. He thought 'I'm so close — I can't let someone else have it.' He bid all the way to HK$245,000. With commission he paid HK$298,900 (~NT$1,196,000) — 50 % over budget. Three months later, the same wine sold at Zachys for HK$185K. He overpaid NT$400,000. **Lesson**: Emotional bidding is the beginner's greatest enemy. Enforce the budget ceiling absolutely. **Case 2 — Ignoring Hidden Costs**: Ms. Chen, 42, business owner. Bought 10 lots, hammer prices totalling HK$120,000 (~NT$480K) — she thought she was within budget. True cost: hammer HK$120,000 (NT$480K); buyer's premium 22 % HK$26,400 (NT$106K) — forgotten!; shipping NY→Taiwan $800 (NT$25K) — forgotten!; insurance 2 %: NT$12K — forgotten!; import duties and tax: NT$60K — forgotten! **Actual total: NT$683,000** — 14 % over budget. **Lesson**: Always calculate: commission + shipping + insurance + taxes — the true cost can be 40–50 % above the hammer price. **Case 3 — Bidding Blind Without Research**: Dr. Wang, 50, physician. He arrived on auction day without studying the catalogue, saw fierce competition and assumed 'if everyone's fighting for it, it must be good', and followed bids blindly. He won 5 lots for NT$350,000. After checking at home: Lot 1 — 2010 Leroy Chambertin (HS condition; overpaid 30 %); Lot 2 — 2012 Dujac Clos de la Roche (village-level, not Grand Cru — he bought the wrong thing!); Lot 3 — the label said 2015, not 2005 as listed; due to the As-Is clause no return was possible; Lots 4 & 5 — ordinary quality, 20 % above market. Dr. Wang lost NT$80,000. **Lesson**: Never follow bids blindly; always research the catalogue and attend the preview; if in doubt, don't buy.
lessons.3.slides.3.title: 🎯 Three Core Bidding Strategies
lessons.3.slides.3.points.0: Sniper strategy: lock onto a few targets; bid decisively when the time comes
lessons.3.slides.3.points.1: Wide-net strategy: multiple alternative lots; bid conservatively; look for bargains
lessons.3.slides.3.points.2: Mixed strategy: 2–3 core targets + 5–10 opportunistic lots
lessons.3.slides.3.points.3: Timing: quieter sessions have less competition; popular sessions have more options
lessons.3.slides.3.points.4: Mental preparation: accept missing a lot; never chase a loss by bidding higher
lessons.3.slides.3.points.5: Long-term thinking: missed today; the opportunity will come again
lessons.3.slides.4.title: Beginner vs Expert Strategy
lessons.3.slides.5.title: Risk Identification and Systematic Management
lessons.3.slides.5.content: **Five Major Risks**: 1️⃣ Authenticity risk (2–5 % probability) — even major auction houses are not 100 % secure; the Rudy Kurniawan counterfeit case (2012) shocked the industry. Mitigation: choose top-tier houses (Sotheby's, Acker); demand provenance; retain 5-year authenticity guarantee documents. 2️⃣ Condition risk (15–20 %) — inability to attend preview; relying solely on catalogue photos; fill level or labels may be worse than expected. Mitigation: **always attend the preview**; photograph everything; choose lots marked 'perfect condition'; avoid 'Inspection Recommended'. 3️⃣ Price risk (30–40 %) — overbidding in hot competition; market price falls after purchase. Mitigation: enforce budget ceiling; research historical prices; avoid popular sessions. 4️⃣ Transport risk (5–10 %) — breakage, loss, temperature fluctuation; international shipping riskier. Mitigation: full insurance; use specialist wine transport; temperature-controlled logistics; track your shipment. 5️⃣ Market risk (long-term) — wine prices fall in recessions; 2008 financial crisis saw auction prices fall 30–40 %; COVID-19 (2020) froze markets briefly. Mitigation: diversify; hold long-term (10+ years); only buy top estates. **Golden Rules**: buy only from major auction houses; insist on perfect condition; demand provenance and storage records; insure everything; retain all documents; deliver immediately to a professional cellar.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: 🎯 Success Story: Auction Wisdom from a Veteran Collector
lessons.3.slides.6.content: **Mr. Huang, 55, entrepreneur, 15 years of auction experience** — He began participating in auctions in 2011 and has built a Burgundy cellar valued at over NT$20 million. His principles: Only buy right; never overpay — 'I'd rather leave empty-handed than overpay for one bottle.' Maintain a dream list of 50 Burgundy Grand Crus, each annotated with a fair-price range; only bid when the auction price falls within the range. Deal with only Acker, Sotheby's, and Zachys; cultivate long-term relationships with specialists for priority preview invitations. In 15 years he has never missed an important preview — even flying to Hong Kong or New York. He has discovered 3 cases where catalogue descriptions did not match the actual bottles. Diversify across 20+ estates; hold for 10+ years before considering a sale; wines purchased in 2015 have since increased in value by 150 %. **Career record (2011–2026)**: participated in ~150 auctions; bid at only ~35; 23 % win rate (highly selective); average buy-in price 15 % below retail at the time; cellar has appreciated approximately 180 %; annualised return ~12 % (outperforming the stock market). **His proudest purchase**: 2016 Acker Hong Kong — 1 bottle of 1990 DRC Romanée-Conti; estimate HK$88,000–110,000; bought at HK$92,000 (with commission HK$112,240); current (2026) market value ~HK$350,000; 10-year appreciation of 212 %. **Advice for newcomers**: don't rush; do your homework; build relationships; enforce discipline; enjoy the process; think long-term; keep learning.
